title: Test the analysis against a truth you planted
subtitle: Interrupted time series, study assumptions, and bounded design certification.
objectives: Interpret the four segmented-regression coefficients and their uncertainty.
Design simulations that challenge an estimator rather than merely exercise it.
Judge bias, coverage, false positives, and power with Monte Carlo uncertainty.
body:
## The simulator and the analysis can fail differently A simulation can implement its mechanisms perfectly while a statistical analysis answers the wrong question. Conversely, an estimator may behave correctly on its assumptions while the simulator makes those assumptions implausibly favorable. Separate the two tasks: verify that the generator creates what it claims, then test whether an analysis recovers a declared target under relevant observation processes. This is why known truth is valuable. We can create an invented series with a known level change, hide that truth from the fitting function, and measure how estimates behave across independent datasets. These arbitrary continuous outcomes are a laboratory for statistical methods. They do not estimate a clinical effect. ## Derive an interrupted time series An interrupted time series, or ITS, compares a trajectory before and after a specified intervention time. The project's segmented model is: ```math Y_t=\beta_0+\beta_1t+\beta_2P_t+\beta_3(t-T)P_t+\varepsilon_t ``` Here Y_t is the observed aggregate outcome, t is time starting at zero, T is the first post-intervention time, P_t is one at and after T and zero beforehand, and epsilon_t is unexplained variation. Beta_0 is the fitted baseline intercept; beta_1 is the pre-intervention slope; beta_2 is the immediate level change at T; beta_3 is the change in slope. The post-intervention slope is beta_1+beta_3. At k periods after the break, the modeled contrast with continuation of the pretrend is: ```math \Delta_k=\beta_2+k\beta_3 ``` Here k=0 corresponds to the break itself. An intervention can have little immediate change yet a substantial later contrast. A test of beta_2 alone therefore does not test every scientifically interesting effect. The [Lopez Bernal, Cummins, and Gasparrini tutorial](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5407170/) provides primary guidance on specifying the expected intervention pattern and examining time-series assumptions. ## Work through a trajectory Take an invented baseline intercept of 20, pretrend of +0.2 units per week, level change of −3, and slope change of −0.1. With T=10, continuing the pretrend predicts 22 at the break; the post-intervention model predicts 19. Five weeks later the contrast is −3.5, because the initial reduction is supplemented by five weeks of changed slope. The post-intervention slope is still positive, +0.1. A rising observed series can therefore coexist with improvement relative to its modeled counterfactual trend.
The lab uses baseline 30 + 0.2t over 48 periods, distinct from the preceding intercept-20 example. Change the level and slope separately, then the break time, coincident change or persistence of its fixed innovation fixture. This is deterministic filtered noise, not a fresh random sample. Ask whether the scientific question concerns the immediate jump, a later contrast, or cumulative change; each requires its own estimate and uncertainty. ## What OLS and HAC do, and what they do not Ordinary least squares, or OLS, chooses coefficients minimizing squared residuals. Correct interpretation needs a suitable mean model and a defensible relationship between predictors and errors. Classical small-sample t inference additionally relies on its error assumptions, including independent, constant-variance normal errors conditional on the design. Adjacent weeks often share shocks, so residuals can be correlated even when observations are neatly separated into rows. Heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation consistent covariance, or HAC, adjusts estimated coefficient uncertainty for certain variance and temporal dependence patterns. It changes the covariance estimate, not the fitted mean trajectory. In this project a positive `hac_maxlags` invokes statsmodels' HAC fit; zero selects the ordinary fit. Its lag choice is part of the method. The [official statsmodels covariance documentation](https://www.statsmodels.org/stable/generated/statsmodels.regression.linear_model.RegressionResults.get_robustcov_results.html) describes these options and the normal-versus-t inference defaults. HAC is an asymptotic device, not insurance against short series, omitted seasonality, changes in outcome definitions, or concurrent interventions. A statistically nonzero pretrend is not itself a failure of ITS: beta_1 explicitly models a pretrend. Instability, misspecification, or an implausible continuation into the postperiod is the concern. Minimum permitted sample sizes merely make a fit computationally possible. Choose observation windows for the process, not for an attractive p-value. Short preperiods poorly reveal seasonal structure; long periods may cross genuine structural changes. A lagged intervention can also violate an instantaneous-break model. Record these design choices before examining success. ## Varying denominators need a scientific choice A mean based on ten people usually contains more individual sampling noise than one based on a hundred. Equal-weight OLS treats each period equally. Weighting by denominator may improve precision under an appropriate individual-noise model, but a shared temporal shock does not shrink merely because more people were observed. A useful hypothetical variance decomposition is: ```math \mathrm{Var}(Y_t)=\sigma_u^2+\frac{\sigma_e^2}{N_t} ``` Here sigma_u squared is period-shock variance, sigma_e squared is individual variance, and N_t is the period denominator; independence assumptions justify adding these terms. Weights proportional to N_t ignore the first term. For counts or proportions, a suitable likelihood or other mean-variance model may be preferable. The current segmented fit is unweighted OLS or OLS with HAC covariance, not an automatic denominator-aware estimator. ## Design the challenge using ADEMP The [Morris, White, and Crowther framework](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6492164/) organizes a simulation study around aims, data-generating mechanisms, estimands, methods, and performance measures—ADEMP. Apply it concretely here: the aim is to assess a level-change estimator; the target is a planted full-population level effect; the methods are specified OLS/HAC variants; the observation mechanisms vary autocorrelation, denominators, seasonality, and selective missingness. The SDK's `ITSDesign` supports these challenges. `generate_design_data` produces independent period cohorts around a population trajectory plus a temporally correlated shock. Its informative-censoring option removes the largest postperiod outcomes. That deliberately changes the observed sample mean relative to the full-population target. An analysis that fits the observed trajectory accurately may consequently estimate the wrong target. ```python from healthcare_sim_sdk.experiments.analysis.certification import ( ITSDesign, DesignCertificationConfig, run_design_certification, ) config = DesignCertificationConfig( designs=(ITSDesign(name="independent", autocorrelation=0.0),), repetitions=100, planted_effect=-0.5, ) report = run_design_certification(config) ``` This is a runnable design specification, not a promised passing result. Each design runs null and nonnull experiments using distinct reproducible seeds. Changing several assumptions together can reveal combined fragility; changing one at a time helps diagnose its cause. ## Judge performance, not the prettiest fitted example Bias is the average estimate minus the planted truth. Root mean squared error combines systematic error and variability: ```math \mathrm{RMSE}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{R}\sum_{r=1}^{R}(\hat{\theta}_r-\theta)^2} ``` Here theta is the known target and theta-hat_r is its estimate in repetition r. Coverage is the fraction of study intervals containing theta. Type I error is the rejection fraction under a true null. Directional power here requires a significant level-change estimate with the planted sign. A biased method can have high power; a wide, uninformative interval can have high coverage. Read these measures together. The current runner saves repetition-level estimates, intervals, p-values, truth, and failures. It reports bias and binary performance summaries with Monte Carlo uncertainty. RMSE is a useful additional calculation from the saved estimates; it is not currently a named certification summary. The upper null false-positive bound must be at or below its configured maximum, and the lower coverage or power bound at or above its configured minimum, before the corresponding gate passes. Bounds straddling a criterion yield `INCONCLUSIVE`. Failed fits do not become an invisible successful-run subset. ## Keep the scope of certification bounded Trying many endpoints, windows, subgroups, and model variants raises the chance of a favorable result. Declare the family of decisions and its multiplicity strategy; a nominal per-fit 5% threshold is not a 5% error rate for the entire search. The same applies when repeatedly adding simulation cells until a method appears acceptable. The harness’s 95% Monte Carlo bounds are pointwise; they do not supply a simultaneous 95% guarantee across every metric and design cell. The package also offers a controlled series contrast and a slope-only monitoring fit. Its controlled helper fits a group-specific linear trajectory and evaluates the group contrast at a selected time; it is not a full pre/post difference-in-differences implementation with automatic identification or dependence handling. Data exports support further study methods, but do not supply those methods themselves. A peer reviewer should match every claim to the design grid that actually ran. A bounded synthetic certification supports estimator behavior under those mechanisms, outcome scales, windows, and thresholds. Unrepresented clinical selection, interference, coding changes, or missing follow-up remain open questions requiring an expanded design or external evidence.

code_refs.claim: Fits the specified four-column segmented model with ordinary or HAC covariance.
Fits a group-specific linear trajectory contrast rather than a complete pre/post DiD model.
Declares bounded synthetic time-series observation designs.
Generates known effects with denominator variation, autocorrelation, seasonality, and selective observation.
Retains per-repetition evidence and evaluates uncertainty-aware performance criteria.

review_questions: Does the reported coefficient correspond to the immediate, later, or cumulative effect we care about?
Which assumptions change when switching OLS covariance to HAC?
What plausible data-generating mechanism was absent from the certification grid?

exercises.question: An ITS has level change −2 and slope change +0.25. What is the modeled contrast eight periods after the break?
exercises.answer: −2 + 8×0.25 = 0. The immediate reduction has disappeared relative to continuation of the fitted pretrend. The contrast requires its own uncertainty calculation using both coefficients and their covariance.

exercises.question: A method rejects 90% of planted-effect runs but also rejects 30% of null runs. Is 90% power enough to recommend it?
exercises.answer: No. High rejection under the null indicates poor false-positive control for that design. Power should be considered alongside null error, bias, coverage, failures, and Monte Carlo precision.
